course.title: Python: from first output to a small feature
course.description: Twelve short lessons across four stages. Predict, run, change one thing, and build a tested study-plan summary. All code runs locally inside the Academy sandbox.
course.assumptions: Start here if you can read short sentences but have never written Python. No packages, terminal commands, account, or online model are needed for the exercises. Use the learning note for predictions and explanations. Optional AI feedback uses your configured model.
stage.0.title: See values
stage.0.goal: Predict output and derive results from inputs.
stage.1.title: Express choices
stage.1.goal: Reuse a function and handle empty and boundary inputs.
stage.2.title: Process records
stage.2.goal: Traverse records and explicitly reject invalid data.
stage.3.title: Build and verify
stage.3.goal: Build a small JSON-producing feature and defend it with counterexamples.
lesson.values.title: Names and visible output
lesson.values.goal: Name two values and show both in program output.
lesson.values.reading:
A program follows the statements you write. In this example, learner names a piece of text and minutes names a whole number. The equals sign assigns a value; it does not ask a question. print makes the current value visible in the output area. Running again starts this small program from the beginning.

Before running, write the two values you expect to see in the learning note. Run the example, compare the output, then change only learner. Which output changes? Text goes between matching quotes; the number does not need quotes. An error message is evidence about the current code, not a judgment about you.

For independent practice, use a name of your choice and a positive number of minutes. The checker accepts your own name and checks that both values appear. After trying yourself, the reference file offers one possible implementation.
lesson.values.exercise: Change learner and minutes. Predict both output lines, run, and explain what assignment changed.
lesson.values.rubric: Show both named values and explain the difference between saving a value and printing it.
lesson.values.question: What does changing learner without changing print do?
lesson.values.observe: The output uses the new learner value.
lesson.values.observe.feedback: print reads the value assigned to that name when it runs.
lesson.values.guess: The output always keeps the original name.
lesson.values.guess.feedback: The name in print is a variable reference, not a copy of the original text.
lesson.values.hint.2: Read the unquoted name inside print.
lesson.calculations.title: Calculate from the inputs
lesson.calculations.goal: Derive a total from two inputs and update it when either input changes.
lesson.calculations.reading:
A computed value records a relationship. unit_minutes * blocks multiplies the current inputs; writing 75 records only one answer. Both versions can look correct for a single example, so one successful run does not prove the relationship.

Predict the total for 25 minutes and three blocks. Run, then change blocks to four. Keep the formula and check whether the result follows your prediction. Now change the unit length. Read the code from the right side of an assignment to the name on the left.

Use integer inputs in this lesson. The checker reads your chosen inputs and calculates the expected total independently. It also checks the displayed result. Describe a different input that could expose a hard-coded answer.
lesson.calculations.exercise: Choose new positive integer inputs, calculate total_minutes with multiplication, and print it.
lesson.calculations.rubric: Use an input-derived calculation and compare at least two input combinations.
lesson.calculations.question: Why try blocks = 4 as well?
lesson.calculations.observe: It can reveal an answer fixed to the first example.
lesson.calculations.observe.feedback: A changed input tests whether the relationship still holds.
lesson.calculations.guess: Repeating the same answer proves every input works.
lesson.calculations.guess.feedback: Repeated output for one input does not cover another input.
lesson.calculations.hint.1: Compare a formula with a constant.
lesson.clean-text.title: Stage task: a clean greeting
lesson.clean-text.goal: Remove outside whitespace and build a greeting from the cleaned name.
lesson.clean-text.reading:
Text values have useful operations. name.strip() returns text with whitespace removed from both ends; it does not change the original name by itself. Store that returned value in clean_name. An f-string places a value inside a template: f"Hello, {clean_name}!".

The starter deliberately keeps the surrounding spaces. Predict what the output will look like before running. Then complete the independent task: clean the name and use it in the greeting. You have the pieces from the first two lessons: names, assignment, and visible output.

Try a name in another language and a name without extra spaces. Explain which value preserves the original input and which holds the cleaned version. This stage task checks a useful relationship rather than one person’s spelling.
lesson.clean-text.exercise: Set clean_name using strip(), then set greeting to Hello, followed by that name and !. Keep the original name.
lesson.clean-text.rubric: Preserve the input, remove only outside whitespace, and print the resulting greeting.
lesson.clean-text.question: Does name.strip() alone replace name?
lesson.clean-text.observe: No. It returns a new value that can be assigned.
lesson.clean-text.observe.feedback: Assignment decides where the returned text is kept.
lesson.clean-text.guess: Yes. Every text operation edits its original input.
lesson.clean-text.guess.feedback: Strings are immutable; this operation returns text instead.
lesson.functions.title: A function that returns a value
lesson.functions.goal: Write and call a function that calculates the duration for any supplied block count.
lesson.functions.reading:
A function packages a relationship so it can be reused with different inputs. In duration(blocks), blocks is a parameter: each call supplies its own value. return sends a result back to the caller. Printing a value displays it, but does not replace returning it.

Predict duration(2), then run the example. Call the same function with zero and with five. The formula still uses a 25-minute block in this lesson; the next lessons will combine functions with choices and collections.

For independent practice, keep the function interface duration(blocks) and make every call return blocks * 25. The checker calls your function with inputs that differ from the example. Explain why a print statement inside the function alone would not satisfy the caller.
lesson.functions.exercise: Return the computed duration and display calls for 0, 2, and 5 blocks.
lesson.functions.rubric: Distinguish parameters, return values, and displayed output.
lesson.functions.question: What does print(duration(2)) print when duration only prints 50 and has no return?
lesson.functions.observe: It also prints None, the function’s implicit return value.
lesson.functions.observe.feedback: A displayed value is separate from a returned value.
lesson.functions.guess: It receives 50 as the function’s return value automatically.
lesson.functions.guess.feedback: print does not turn the displayed value into the function result.
lesson.functions.hint.2: Use return for a computed function result.
lesson.decisions.title: Choose a branch
lesson.decisions.goal: Use an inclusive threshold and explain its boundary case.
lesson.decisions.reading:
A condition selects which block runs. In ready(minutes), the rule is to return True for at least 20 minutes and False otherwise. The comparison >= includes exactly 20; > would exclude it. Indentation marks the body of the if statement and the function.

Predict ready(19), ready(20), and ready(21) before running. Only one boundary character changes the middle answer. A boolean such as True describes a yes-or-no result; it is different from the text "True".

For independent practice, keep the rule and return actual booleans for each input. Explain the boundary in ordinary words. The checker includes the boundary and values on both sides, so it can expose a condition that happens to work for the displayed example.
lesson.decisions.exercise: Implement ready(minutes): at least 20 returns True, less returns False. Try 19, 20, and 21.
lesson.decisions.rubric: State the threshold, include equality, and return booleans rather than strings.
lesson.decisions.question: Which input separates > 20 from >= 20?
lesson.decisions.observe.feedback: Both comparisons agree on 19 and 21; they disagree on equality.
lesson.decisions.guess.feedback: 21 is above the threshold for both comparisons.
lesson.decisions.hint.2: Read “at least” as including the threshold.
lesson.sequences.title: Stage task: first task or a fallback
lesson.sequences.goal: Read the first list element while handling an empty list without modifying the input.
lesson.sequences.reading:
A list keeps values in order. Index zero selects its first element. An empty list has no first element, so tasks[0] would raise IndexError. In a condition, an empty list is false and a nonempty list is true.

The starter works for the displayed list but not for an empty list. Predict both cases. Combine the previous lesson’s branch with indexing: return the first task if one exists, otherwise return "rest". Do not remove the task from the original list.

This is a transfer task: no new control structure is needed. Try a one-item list and a longer list after the empty case. The checker verifies both the result and the unchanged input, because reading and consuming a task are different operations.
lesson.sequences.exercise: Implement first_task(tasks), returning "rest" for [] and the first task otherwise. Leave tasks unchanged.
lesson.sequences.rubric: Cover empty and nonempty inputs and explain why the fallback must precede indexing.
lesson.sequences.question: Why guard tasks[0]?
lesson.sequences.observe: An empty list has no element at index zero.
lesson.sequences.observe.feedback: The branch avoids indexing when no item exists.
lesson.sequences.guess: Index zero always creates a missing element.
lesson.sequences.guess.feedback: Reading an index does not create a list item.
lesson.loops.title: Accumulate a list of durations
lesson.loops.goal: Use a for loop to total every item, including an empty input.
lesson.loops.reading:
A for loop visits list values in order. Start total at zero, then add each duration with total = total + minutes. Keep the accumulator inside the function, so each call starts fresh. return belongs after the loop; placing it inside would stop after the first item.

Predict the running totals for [10, 20, 5]. Write each intermediate total in your note, then compare the final output. An empty list performs no iterations and leaves the total at zero.

Try a single item and call the function twice. Independent checks include empty and unequal durations, so neither a fixed answer nor “number of items times the first duration” can satisfy the contract. Explain how you know every item contributed exactly once.
lesson.loops.exercise: Implement total_minutes(durations) with a fresh accumulator; compare [], [7], and [10, 20, 5].
lesson.loops.rubric: Explain initialization, one contribution per item, and return after the loop.
lesson.loops.question: What does an empty list total to here?
lesson.loops.observe.feedback: No iterations change the initial accumulator.
lesson.loops.guess: It must use the previous call’s total.
lesson.loops.guess.feedback: The accumulator is local and initialized on every call.
lesson.loops.hint.2: The initial total is already the empty sum.
lesson.records.title: Give a record meaningful fields
lesson.records.goal: Read a named field and distinguish a missing field from a false value.
lesson.records.reading:
A dictionary associates keys with values. A task can have a title and a done flag. task.get("done", False) reads the flag or uses a default only when that key is absent. Keys such as "done" are text, not variable names.

Run the two records in the example and predict which title goes into the result. This function gathers titles of tasks whose done value is exactly False. A missing done field uses False, while a completed task is left out.

Add a third record of your own. Keep the inputs unchanged and preserve their order in the output list. Explain the difference between an empty result list and a failure to process input. The checker uses different titles so your function must read each record.
lesson.records.exercise: Implement pending_titles(tasks): return titles with done False or missing, preserving order and inputs.
lesson.records.rubric: Read named fields, apply the documented default, and avoid mutating records.
lesson.records.question: When does get("done", False) use its default?
lesson.records.observe: When the done key is absent.
lesson.records.observe.feedback: A present False is an existing value; it is not a missing key.
lesson.records.guess.feedback: get checks the requested key, not every field’s truth value.
lesson.validation.title: Stage task: reject an invalid duration
lesson.validation.goal: Accept only nonnegative integers and reject booleans, text, and negative values explicitly.
lesson.validation.reading:
A function contract can reject input instead of inventing an answer. raise ValueError("minutes") reports an invalid value to its caller. In Python, bool is related to int, so type(value) is int is useful for this lesson’s exact integer contract.

The starter currently returns every input unchanged. Predict what it would accept incorrectly. Add a condition before the return: the value must be an exact integer and at least zero. Preserve valid zero; do not use if not value to reject it.

Test one valid value, the boundary zero, and one rejected example of each kind. A rejection is part of correct behavior here. The checker catches ValueError and fails if an invalid input silently becomes a valid result. The reference shows one implementation after your attempt.
lesson.validation.exercise: Complete validate_minutes(value). Return valid nonnegative integers; otherwise raise ValueError.
lesson.validation.rubric: Cover zero, negatives, booleans, text, and a normal valid value without coercing invalid inputs.
lesson.validation.question: Why is if not value insufficient?
lesson.validation.observe: It rejects valid zero and misses some invalid types.
lesson.validation.observe.feedback: Truthiness does not express the complete type-and-range contract.
lesson.validation.guess: All false values must be invalid durations.
lesson.validation.guess.feedback: Zero is an allowed duration under this contract.
lesson.validation.hint.2: Reject when type(value) is not int or value < 0.
lesson.json-data.title: Round-trip a small record
lesson.json-data.goal: Encode a record as JSON text and decode it without losing Unicode or zero.
lesson.json-data.reading:
JSON is a text format for exchanging data. json.dumps turns a Python value into text; json.loads parses JSON text into a Python value. An imported standard-library module supplies these operations. A JSON string is not already a dictionary, even if its displayed characters look similar.

Predict the type before encoding and after decoding. The example uses ensure_ascii=False so Unicode characters remain readable in the text. That setting changes representation, not the underlying name.

For independent practice, implement round_trip(record) and return the decoded value. Try a record containing a non-English title and minutes equal to zero. The checker checks values and the unchanged original record. This lesson exchanges data in memory and does not read or write your files.
lesson.json-data.exercise: Implement round_trip(record) with json.dumps and json.loads. Compare the original and returned record.
lesson.json-data.rubric: Distinguish a Python object from serialized text and preserve supported data values.
lesson.json-data.question: What does json.dumps return?
lesson.json-data.observe.feedback: Parsing that string is a separate step.
lesson.json-data.guess.feedback: Encoding produces a textual representation, not the original object.
lesson.json-data.hint.2: Use type(encoded) in a small experiment.
lesson.test-cases.title: Explain a test with a counterexample
lesson.test-cases.goal: Write checks for normal, boundary, and rejected input, and show that a broken implementation fails.
lesson.test-cases.reading:
An assert compares observed behavior with an expected result. If the condition is false it raises AssertionError. In a try/except block, a matching exception is evidence that the rejected-input rule was followed; reaching the line after the block without rejection is a different outcome.

The test function receives an implementation as its parameter. This lets you test both a working validator and one that simply returns its input. Predict which assertion exposes the broken version.

Add checks for zero, a normal integer, a negative number, a boolean, and text. Do not catch every exception: only ValueError satisfies the input contract. The independent checker supplies several broken implementations to your test function. A test that accepts everything is not useful evidence.
lesson.test-cases.exercise: Complete check_validator(candidate) so it accepts a correct validator and raises AssertionError for broken ones.
lesson.test-cases.rubric: Include valid and rejected cases, catch the specified error only, and demonstrate a failing counterexample.
lesson.test-cases.question: Does a test that never fails distinguish a broken validator?
lesson.test-cases.observe: No. It needs a case with an independently expected outcome.
lesson.test-cases.observe.feedback: The expectation must not be copied from the candidate’s own result.
lesson.test-cases.guess: Yes. Finishing the test is sufficient evidence.
lesson.test-cases.guess.feedback: A completed test without behavioral assertions may accept every implementation.
lesson.test-cases.hint.1: Try a function that always returns zero.
lesson.test-cases.hint.2: A normal valid value should stay unchanged.
lesson.study-plan.title: Final task: a study-plan summary
lesson.study-plan.goal: Combine validation, records, loops, and JSON into one bounded data transformation.
lesson.study-plan.reading:
Build a small feature from the pieces you now know. summarize(tasks) receives task records containing title, minutes, and done. It returns JSON text with pending_count and pending_minutes. Only tasks whose done flag is False contribute. A missing done flag uses False. Every record’s minutes must be validated, even when that task is already complete.

The starter validates each record but returns zeros. Run it and explain why successful execution is not yet the requested behavior. Then implement the two accumulators. An empty plan is valid and has zero pending tasks and minutes. Preserve all input records.

Try your own plan after the supplied example. Use the checklist you developed: ordinary inputs, an empty list, a zero-duration task, a completed task, and invalid minutes. Explain the evidence behind your result in the learning note. A checker pass covers this contract, not every possible planning application.
lesson.study-plan.exercise: Return JSON with exact fields pending_count and pending_minutes; validate all minutes and preserve input records.
lesson.study-plan.rubric: Meet the documented contract, cover empty and rejected cases, and explain a new plan without copying the example.
lesson.study-plan.question: Why validate minutes on a completed task?
lesson.study-plan.observe: The contract applies to every input record.
lesson.study-plan.observe.feedback: Filtering contributions does not remove the input-validity requirement.
lesson.study-plan.guess: A completed flag makes every other field valid.
lesson.study-plan.guess.feedback: A status flag is not evidence that another field has a valid type and range.
